summary:
No one will ever visit another star. Last year, a piece of one visited us. A frozen stranger, possibly older than the Earth, had drifted alone through the dark for billions of years to get here. Comet 3I/ATLAS is leaving now. No one alive will see it again.

NASA’s SPHEREx telescope caught its goodbye. In most of the telescope’s 102 colours you would never spot it, but slide to 4.27 microns, where carbon dioxide glows, and it bursts into view. Press play to watch it travel.

Now close your eyes. It’s gone. That is how millions of blind and low-vision people meet the universe: as pictures they can’t reach.

So we built Ashesha, Sanskrit for “without remainder”. We gave the comet a sound, silent until it appears, then swelling with its light. Every picture has words, and Selene, goddess of the Moon, guides you one calm step at a time.

The whole sky opens: the fastest-crawling star we know, a giant that pulses, any patch you choose. Notice something? Mark it as a candidate.

It crossed the dark between stars to visit us once. Everyone deserves to say goodbye.
details:
What it does

Ashesha plays NASA’s SPHEREx survey back like a flipbook. Pick a patch of sky and every SPHEREx picture of that spot plays in date order, with a Then and Now strip of small pictures underneath. Stars hold still. Anything that moves or changes stands out.

We prepared six targets: the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS and the challenge’s five test targets (Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis). Together that is 1,838 SPHEREx images from the QR2 release. You can also type in your own right ascension and declination, and the site asks IRSA for a few images of that spot.

The comet is our headline. SPHEREx takes each picture in a single colour of infrared light, and a colour slider walks you through them. In August 2025, on the way in, the comet shows up in our pictures only in a narrow band near 4.27 microns, where the SPHEREx team reported a cloud of carbon dioxide around it. In December, after its closest pass to the Sun, it is brighter and we see it in dozens of colours. You can watch it wake up.

Each picture gets one of four labels: clear detection, faint, not detected, or no observation. Each label has its own shape, so colour is never the only clue. Open a label and you see the date, wavelength, detector and any contamination flags, plus a link to the original file at IRSA. If something looks odd, you can mark the picture as a candidate. Your list stays in your browser, and you can export it.

How it works

Our data pipeline is written in Python. For a given position it asks IRSA’s TAP service for every SPHEREx image that covers it, follows each DataLink record to the image file, and downloads a small cutout instead of the full frame. It measures the brightness at the target, works out a signal to noise ratio, and picks the label: 10 or more counts as clear, 3 or more as faint. It also builds median stacks for each of SPHEREx’s six detectors, early dates and late dates, because stacking pulls faint objects out of the noise. For the comet we re-centred each cutout on IRSA’s predicted position before stacking. The stars smear out and the comet stays sharp.

The pipeline writes plain JSON and PNG files, and the website reads them. There is no server and no framework, only HTML, CSS and JavaScript hosted on GitHub Pages. Each data file records its SPHEREx release. When a new release comes out, we re-run the script for each target and commit the new files, and the site code stays as it is. Links carry the target or the coordinates (for example ?target=3I-ATLAS), so anyone can share or embed a view.

Around the viewer sit smaller rooms, and each has a guide from Greek myth. Selene, goddess of the Moon, gives the site tour. She also teaches Spot a candidate, a short lesson on when a picture deserves a second look; its trick examples come from real SPHEREx pictures, and Elisabetta, our data lead, checked each answer. Iris, goddess of the rainbow, runs Cryostella, four short steps on reading a spectrum, hearing one, and telling a cold cloud from a comet by ear. Orpheus leads the Cosmic Orchestra, where the data turns into sound. In Your Beginnings you enter your birthday and see the ring of sky SPHEREx photographed on that date, and which famous objects it caught.

Why it matters

The WHO counts at least 2.2 billion people with a near or distance vision impairment. WebAIM’s 2025 scan of the top million home pages found accessibility failures that a machine can detect on 94.8% of them, and images with no description on 55.5%. For a blind visitor, a space website full of pictures is mostly silence.

We designed Ashesha for blind, low-vision, colour-blind, deaf and neurodivergent visitors from the first sketch. Each picture has a written description in a fixed order: number, date, colour, label and note. The viewer also turns the comet’s predicted positions into sentences such as “Since image 3, the comet’s predicted position moved right by about 6 percent of the picture’s width.” A data table carries the same facts as the strip. The colour slider tells a screen reader what the comet is doing at that colour, in words. We wrote a meaning next to each sound, and sound stops while the screen reader is speaking. Nothing plays or moves until you press a button, and the site respects reduced motion settings. There are no timers and no login, and nothing you do leaves your browser.

We hope a person who has never been invited into astronomy will follow a real comet here and mark their first candidate. The repository is public under the MIT licence, so another team can reuse the access patterns for their own data.

What makes it creative

The name came first. Ashesha is Sanskrit for “without remainder”. Our logo turns the A upside down into ∀, the mathematician’s symbol for “for all”, and a comet makes the crossbar.

We gave the 102 colours a job. In a mission description they are a number. On Ashesha they are a slider, and sliding it is the main moment, because that is where the comet appears.

The guides talk. We drew each one from a portrait the team made with Google Gemini, and a small WebGL rig moves the mouth while the browser’s own voice reads the step aloud. Visitors who use a screen reader can switch the voice off.

The home page opens with a blink game: two pictures, flicked back and forth, find the one that jumped. That is how Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930. Our team cards show each person’s constellation, drawn from real star positions.

What we considered

We wrote ourselves a set of honest rules before writing any code. We say “candidate”, never “discovery”, because only experts confirm discoveries. We call the sound “a sonification: sounds mapped by rules we chose”, since a comet makes no sound we could record. WISE 0855 is a faint brown dwarf, and our pipeline labels it “not detected” in 252 of its 256 pictures. The site tells you that straight. We tested subtracting early pictures from late ones and dropped it: the background swamped the result, and the site explains why. Because each SPHEREx picture is a different colour, the site also warns that a change in brightness between two pictures is not always a real change.

We also planned for a judge with two minutes. The examples work in one click, and Selene’s tour starts only when you ask for it. The site works on a 375 pixel wide phone and at 400% zoom. We used Atkinson Hyperlegible, a typeface the Braille Institute designed for low-vision readers. Our colour-blind theme uses the Okabe-Ito palette, and we checked the four status colours in a simulation of three kinds of colour blindness. We credit the data with IRSA’s acknowledgement text and the release DOI (10.26131/IRSA652). This project is not endorsed by NASA or IRSA.

A few things went wrong along the way. Our first test notebook searched a fixed position, so its “comet” results showed the WISE 0855 field and not the comet. IRSA often answered with temporary 503 errors, so every request now tries again on its own. And in August the comet hid in most single pictures, which is what pushed us toward stacks and the colour slider.

Tools we used

Data: Python, Astropy, astroquery, NumPy and Google Colab, with IRSA’s TAP, DataLink and cutout services and the SPHEREx QR2 release.

Website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework, SVG, WebGL, the Web Audio API and the Web Speech API, hosted on GitHub Pages. We tested with keyboard only and with the NVDA screen reader.

AI: Claude Code (Anthropic) helped us write and review code. Google Gemini made the guides’ portraits from prompts we wrote. We logged each use in docs/ai-use-log.md.

Hardware: just our own laptops.
